body: Two men meet at a motorway services on the second Tuesday of the month, because it is roughly halfway and neither of them has to do the whole drive. They have been doing this for eleven years. One buys the coffee, the other buys it next time, and they sit at the same table by the window with the car park in front of them. They talk about a gearbox, a football result, whether the eldest will get the grades. Then, at about the eighty-minute mark, usually while one of them is putting his coat on, somebody says the real thing. Ten minutes later they are back in their cars. Neither of them has ever given this arrangement a name.

That table is a means of grace, and both men would be embarrassed to hear it called one. It has no leader, no curriculum and no end date, and it has kept two households upright through a redundancy, a diagnosis and a son who stopped speaking to his father for two years.

The classic list is well covered. Prayer, the reading of Scripture, the sacraments, fasting, giving — the practices through which grace is understood to reach a person, all taught, all preached, all with centuries of literature behind them.

The phrase itself is worth slowing down on, because it is more generous than the way it is usually used. A means is a channel. It is not a fee and it is not a performance; it is the ordinary furniture God has chosen to move through, and the whole point of the doctrine is that grace comes by things rather than by achievements — by water, by bread, by wine, by words read aloud by somebody who did not write them. Nothing on that list is impressive in itself. Bread is not holy. It is a means. Once that is admitted, it becomes very hard to explain, on the theology, why a person who keeps turning up should not be on the list too. A friend is at least as ordinary as bread.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today. One of them is Walking Together at HM 397.60 — fellowship teaching, small-group depth in a station that runs all day. It is assigned, it is in build, and it is not yet on air.

That the number is held for it at all is the argument in miniature. A frequency here belongs to one station permanently and can never be recycled, so reserving one for something as unglamorous as company is a real cost, paid in a stretch of dial a livelier format would have taken. It is paid because of what happens when you ask the question directly. Ask somebody what sustained them through the worst decade of their life and you will very rarely be told about a discipline. You will be told a name.

The Church is oddly quiet about this, and the quietness is not accidental. Friendship cannot be programmed, rota’d or measured, and institutions are built to do exactly those three things. So it gets translated into vocabulary the institution can handle — accountability, fellowship, community, small groups — all of which describe something narrower, more official and less durable than what people mean when they say my friend. A church can start a group on Thursday. It cannot start a friendship, and it knows it, so it talks about the thing it can start.

Scripture is much less shy. David and Jonathan takes up a great deal of space for a relationship with no institutional function whatever — Jonathan holds no office in David’s life, and the covenant between them accomplishes nothing administrative. Ruth’s speech, the one read at weddings, is said to a mother-in-law on a road. And Paul cannot stop naming people. The ends of his letters are lists of individuals, and those lists are the part everybody skips. In one of them he stops to remember a man who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chain. That is not a job title. That is a friend, remembered in the middle of an epistle.
So the pattern is right there in the text, and we read past it because it does not look like a doctrine.

The structures deserve a fair hearing before they are set aside. A small group on a Wednesday is a real good, and for somebody who has just moved to a city it may be the only door there is. Accountability arrangements have kept men out of trouble that would have cost them their marriages. But everything organised has a term. The group runs for six weeks, the rota rotates, the curriculum finishes and the pastor who set it up moves on. The people who show up came because they were asked, and they stop when they are no longer asked, and none of that is a failure of character. It is what organised things do. A friend has no term, was never asked, and cannot be reassigned.
Which is why the answer is a name and not a programme.

For two years, while her friend’s marriage came apart in slow motion, a woman went round every Thursday after work. She did not counsel. She brought a bag of shopping — bread, milk, the biscuits the children liked — put the kettle on and stayed two hours, and most of those Thursdays they watched whatever happened to be on and talked about almost nothing. She never once asked how the divorce was going. She did not bring a verse. She just kept arriving at about six with the same blue carrier bag, on a day of the week that had stopped meaning anything else. Years later the friend said, to somebody else, in a car park, that she would not be here, and did not elaborate, because she did not need to.

Notice what that woman had that a professional could not have. Not skill. Continuity, and no agenda, and the fact that she already knew the whole situation and never needed it re-explained from the beginning.

There is a real cost to arguing this, and it should be stated without softening. If friendship is a means of grace, then some people are being starved of grace by circumstance, which is a considerably bleaker thing to say than most sermons on the subject go anywhere near. You cannot instal a friend. You cannot resolve to have one by Friday. People move, people get ill, people work shifts that make ordinary company impossible, and a great many faithful people are alone on a Thursday evening and did nothing to deserve it. And it must be said plainly that a radio station is not a friend and will never be one. It does not know your name, it cannot ring you back, and it will not notice if you stop.

But look at how the friendships you have actually acquired began, because it was almost never by decision. It was proximity, repetition, and something in common in the background — a job, a school gate, a team, a record you both happened to love. Nobody sets out to make a friend. They set out to do something else, near somebody, more than once. Shared attention is the raw material, and it has become scarce, because everybody is now served a private feed and two people in one room are rarely listening to the same thing at the same second. A dial is one of the last formats where they are. That is thin company, admittedly. But thin company is how thick company starts, and nothing thick has ever started any other way.

So put friendship where the theology already implies it belongs. Not as a social bonus for the fortunate, and not as a delivery mechanism for advice, but as one of the ordinary channels through which God has evidently chosen to work, alongside the bread and the water and the words. It is the one on the list that nobody teaches and nobody schedules, and it is the one that gets named when somebody is asked what actually saved them.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing.

The dial carries four kinds of programming — music, which is most of the band; teaching and prayer; family programming; and the international stations in their own languages. The stations built specifically around company are mostly still coming: Walking Together at HM 397.60, Iron Sharpening Iron at HM 386.20, Pure Heart Brothers at HM 396.20, all assigned, all in build, and none of them on air yet. So the recommendation is a music station, and the reason is the format rather than the subject matter.

Put on HM 315.20 — Corner Cipher. It is on air now. Christian rap out of Atlanta, Marcus Reed on the microphone, trap and lyrical and soul-gospel, talking about the block he actually came from. The reason it belongs at the end of this particular article is in its name. A cipher is a circle. People stand in a ring and take turns, and the ones not rapping are holding the thing up. There is no version of it you can do alone — the form does not exist without other people, and every record in that tradition is a record of company. You may not be its audience. That is the format doing its job rather than failing at it, and fifteen minutes of a circle you were not born into is a fair swap for an argument about friendship.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen if you like. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the ones still in build get their opening dates.

So here is the invitation, and it comes in two halves. Put HM 315.20 on this afternoon and let it play whether or not you chose it. Then, while it is on, text the person whose name you would give if somebody asked you what got you through — the one you have been meaning to ring since about March. Suggest a coffee somewhere halfway. That is the whole application of this article, it takes about forty seconds, and it is the only means of grace on the list that will not happen unless one of you goes first.
